surveyDefinition.title: Skin Care Products — consumer survey (India)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routine complexity, purchase drivers, product expectations, and switching triggers.

segments.name: Routine Minimalists
segments.description: Use 1-3 basic products (cleanser, moisturizer, sunscreen) on a simple daily schedule. Driven by convenience and basic skin health, not by chasing specific concerns. Low engagement with ingredients or claims; buy on habit or price.

segments.name: Concern-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Have one or two specific skin concerns (aging, acne, hyperpigmentation) and actively research products targeting those concerns. Willing to pay more for clinically proven efficacy and visible results. Routine is moderately complex and tailored to their concern.

segments.name: Safety-First Consumers
segments.description: Prioritize gentle, non-irritating, and 'clean' formulations. Often have sensitive skin or worry about long-term chemical exposure. Heavily influenced by dermatologist recommendations and transparent ingredient lists. Routine may be simple but deliberately chosen for safety.

segments.name: High-Engagement Users
segments.description: Treat skincare as a hobby or self-care ritual. Use multi-step routines (5+ products), follow trends (K-beauty, actives), and enjoy experimenting. High spend, high brand awareness, and open to switching for novelty or better results.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Skin Care Products buyers in India. It asks how people use Skin Care Products, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in India who buy or use Skin Care Products for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. Excluded: Professional buyers (e.g., dermatology clinics, spas, salons) purchasing for resale or professional use; Individuals purchasing solely as gifts for others; Children under 18.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
respondentBehaviours: Regularly purchases skin care products (e.g., cleansers, moisturizers, serums, sunscreens)
Researches products online, reads reviews, follows influencers or dermatologist recommendations
May have specific skin concerns (acne, aging, sensitivity, hyperpigmentation)
Brand loyal but open to switching for better efficacy or price
Purchases through multiple channels: drugstores, department stores, specialty beauty retailers, e-commerce, subscription boxes
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's current skincare landscape — what products they use, how complex their routine is, and what skin concerns they are managing. It then traces their purchase journey from trigger through discovery, channel, and decision drivers, ending with spend. Next, it probes their product expectations — must-haves, quality cues, claims, formats, and trade-offs — before closing with satisfaction, unmet needs, and switching triggers. This arc cleanly separates the four segments: Routine Minimalists (low complexity, low engagement), Concern-Driven Optimizers…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Skin Care Products in India — who Individuals who have purchased at least one skin care product for personal use in the past 12 months; Primary decision-maker for their own skin care purchases; Ages 18 and older. The audience is defined as the end consumer who buys and uses skin care products for personal care. This captures the core B2C market and allows for segmentation by demographics, skin concerns, and purchasing behavior.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on skincare routine complexity, purchase drivers, product expectations, and switching triggers.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural (routine complexity and frequency) and jobs-to-be-done (the primary skin concern the routine is hired to solve). This fits because skincare buyers differ fundamentally in how involved their routine is (simple vs multi-step) and what they are hiring the products to do

segments.name: Routine Minimalists
segments.description: Use 1-3 basic products (cleanser, moisturizer, sunscreen) on a simple daily schedule. Driven by convenience and basic skin health, not by chasing specific concerns. Low engagement with ingredients or claims; buy on habit or price.
segments.hypothesis: They will report low routine complexity, low spend, and low interest in clinical claims; they switch mainly on price or availability.

segments.name: Concern-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Have one or two specific skin concerns (aging, acne, hyperpigmentation) and actively research products targeting those concerns. Willing to pay more for clinically proven efficacy and visible results. Routine is moderately complex and tailored to their concern.
segments.hypothesis: They will score high on 'targeted solutions' and 'clinically proven efficacy' as purchase drivers, and will switch brands if a competitor offers better evidence of results.

segments.name: Safety-First Consumers
segments.description: Prioritize gentle, non-irritating, and 'clean' formulations. Often have sensitive skin or worry about long-term chemical exposure. Heavily influenced by dermatologist recommendations and transparent ingredient lists. Routine may be simple but deliberately chosen for safety.
segments.hypothesis: They will rank 'skin compatibility' and 'natural/safe ingredients' above efficacy, and will reject products with harsh chemicals even if they work well.

segments.name: High-Engagement Users
segments.description: Treat skincare as a hobby or self-care ritual. Use multi-step routines (5+ products), follow trends (K-beauty, actives), and enjoy experimenting. High spend, high brand awareness, and open to switching for novelty or better results.
segments.hypothesis: They will report the highest routine complexity, highest spend, and strongest interest in new formats and personalized solutions; they are the most likely to try new brands.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question that best settles a tie is cp2 ('Which of these best describes your skincare routine?') because it directly asks respondents to self-report their overall routine complexity, which is the most distinguishing behavioural difference between the segments (minimalist vs. multi-step).
notes: Routine minimalists are identified by simple routines, convenience, price sensitivity, and habit-based repurchase.
Concern-driven optimizers are identified by specific concerns, clinical proof, and visible results.
Safety-first consumers are identified by sensitivity, dermatologist trust, and clean/fragrance-free preferences.
High-engagement enthusiasts are identified by multi-step routines, trend-following, frequent purchases, and high spend.
5 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by mapping the respondent's current skincare landscape — what products they use, how complex their routine is, and what skin concerns they are managing. It then traces their purchase journey from trigger through discovery, channel, and decision drivers, ending with spend. Next, it probes their product expectations — must-haves, quality cues, claims, formats, and trade-offs — before closing with satisfaction, unmet needs, and switching triggers. This arc cleanly separates the four segments: Routine Minimalists (low complexity, low engagement), Concern-Driven Optimizers…
storyline_notes: Replaced generic 'usage frequency' with 'routine complexity' as a core beat, because in skincare the number of steps is a stronger differentiator than simple frequency.
Added 'skin concerns' as a distinct beat in the profile section to capture the jobs-to-be-done lens — the specific problem the routine is hired to solve.
In buying behavior, placed 'decision drivers' before 'spend' to build up to the sensitive money question, and included 'dermatologist recommendation' as a key driver given the APAC pharmacy culture.

In preferences, added 'claims and credentials' early to reflect the region's growing concern for ingredient transparency and clinical evidence, and kept 'value expectation' last as the most sensitive.

In the final section, merged 'advocacy' into 'satisfaction drivers' to stay within the question budget, and focused on 'switching' and 'future use' to capture the high-growth, high-switching APAC market.
All beats are answerable with closed questions and avoid age, income, geography, and brand names, per the constraints.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy skin care products for personal use, pay for them out of pocket at retail or online, and make the purchase decision themselves. While some professional products are sold to salons, the dominant consumer market is direct-to-consumer, so this is a pure B2C segment.
